title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [15:00]
label: developer
claim: Telegraphed attacks: all enemy attacks are shown, 'there's no miss chance and there's no hit chance', so the information is always accurate and the player turn is deterministic; the only randomness is the enemy choosing position and target. He says it 'ended up shaping the entire game' and 'breaks every other tactics system we were used to'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [15:00]
label: developer
claim: Telegraphing removed the core of tactics games: threat management ('90% of the tactics game was about managing the threat') becomes trivial because you just step out of the shown zone. Fix was making immovable buildings the thing enemies target and the thing you lose by, so threat still has teeth.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [24:00]
label: developer
claim: Goal was a chess-like interface: 'you don't need to mouse over the pawn to double check what it does'; each puzzle should be plannable 'without double-checking everything on the board'. Early iterations without icons 'was a mess'; it 'spent years to add the icons and figure out which ones we needed', some added 'as late as just like three months before release'; icons 'looked so painfully obvious in hindsight' but playtesters were confused, remove/restore repeated 'ad nauseam for years'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [25:00]
label: developer
claim: What to show was learned by iteration: they first thought showing the target of each enemy was enough, but 'the attack type was also important to show' because moving a unit changes whether it punches or shoots a tile. Showing target plus type 'hugely constrained the possibilities' of the design.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [26:00]
label: developer
claim: Cutting content to fit the UI: 'instead of building a UI [that] could describe all of our weapons we had to start building weapons that could be described by the UI'. Limited to three attack types (artillery, melee, projectile); abandoned radius threat ranges and four-leaf-clover attack shapes (the Tetris-like layering idea) because you could not tell what threatened what.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [27:00]
label: developer
claim: Orthogonal-only attacks: shooting up, down, left or right meant 'if you knew what places you could move to then you knew where you could shoot', and enemies lined up with their attacks so it was 'much easier at a glance to see what enemy is attacking where'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [28:00]
label: developer
claim: Static enemy designs for readability: 'once the player has learned the units the units are reliably the same'. A Firefly upgraded to a version that also pushed its target was 'really hard to remember and keep track of', so upgraded (purple) units only get more health, damage and movement. Side effect: push attacks almost vanished from enemies; weapon upgrade trees by the artist were ditched. Cost: no micro-tuning of difficulty, since every enemy is fixed.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [22:00]
label: developer
claim: Randomness added back deliberately: 'we need a miss chance'. A low-percentage grid-defense chance means a building may not be damaged, so when a checkmate-like situation arises ('a dead turn ... might as well be a I lose button') the player can 'cross the fingers and hit end turn'. Players 'really hated' the pilot grid-defense skill; he says he would make it near-hidden in hindsight.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [21:00]
label: developer
claim: Progress and goals: win by surviving a turn limit rather than killing everything, because manipulating telegraphed enemies is more fun than killing them. The fail state is the power grid (buildings power the mechs); he calls the narrative wrapper 'the least bad option' and says 'I don't even think we really explained it very well in the game'; the player just 'sees it says power grid that sounds important'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [19:00]
label: developer
claim: Turn limit gives streamlining: no dead turns hunting the last enemy, so 'impactful in every turn'. Battles are 'only four or five turns'; he would have said four-turn battles 'sounds really hard' if asked up front, but it fell out of the telegraphed-attack constraints.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [36:00]
label: developer
claim: Progress clarity in the strategy layer: they wanted an unambiguous fail state ('a health bar ... can show you where your fail state lies') so players play to the end and 'always thought they had a chance', versus Civ-style ambiguous losses where people quit; the final strategy layer cut everything down to 'one choice' between missions with clear rewards.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [42:00]
label: developer
claim: Strategy screen readability: three resources (power, upgrade cores, money), difficulty shown by resource count, and a single-screen UI where 'without checking tooltips ... you can see instantly what your choices are'. Earlier asset system cut partly because one option was always 'ten times better than the rest', which 'is not an interesting choice'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [44:00]
label: developer
claim: A progress choice that confused: player-chosen game length (end after two islands or continue to four) was meant as pure player choice, but buried in a strategy game the choice got muddled (auto-caption garbled), and forum players hunted for the optimal time to attack the boss, though the boss scales to the same difficulty regardless. He is 'not 100% sure I would chase it down again'.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [46:00]
label: developer
claim: Difficulty in a puzzle game: 'too hard becomes unsolvable instead of just hard'; with six attackers and three mechs 'you just can't stop' it and the game feels unfair, so spawn rules and map design are built to keep every board solvable. Difficulty was 'constrained by the design': 'this is how hard it can be' rather than a chosen target.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [47:00]
label: developer
claim: Teaching gap: early Steam reviews split between 'way too hard' and 'way too easy'. In playtests people 'didn't want to get their units hurt' and did not want to defend buildings, so the game's central decisions were 'not necessarily intuitive'; he says 'maybe we did a bad job teaching that and explaining it ahead of time'. No explicit tutorial text discussed.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [48:00]
label: developer
claim: Disputes 'hard games are better': 'if you told me 10 years ago that an easy game could be super fun my naive early designer self would have said that's silly'. Puzzle design benefits from easy play like a crossword you are good at, while easy FTL was dull because you felt pandered to.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [52:00]
label: developer
claim: Q&A on randomness/assist: he does not rig the grid-defense odds ('we don't try to artificially create those exciting saves'), preferring static board-game-like rules that do not accommodate the player. The one exception is spawn count: enemies are bumped up if too few and dropped if too many, the only place the game checks board state and adjusts.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [54:00]
label: developer
claim: Q&A on onboarding: the starting squad was 'still too complex for a lot of players', especially an artillery weapon you shoot next to an enemy to push it, because 'all games have always trained us to shoot at the enemy'. Focus became introducing push in 'a very natural way' so everyone could try the starting squad.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [56:00]
label: developer
claim: Simple AI, hand-made maps: each enemy acts independently, picks best and second-best options and randomizes between them. About 200 maps are pre-made (not procedural) because a bad map 'could really influence the difficulty in ways that were horrible' and they needed tight control.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [49:00]
label: developer
claim: Disputes 'perfect every mechanic': 'there can be mediocre design in the game'; they were 'overly perfectionist' and learned a designer sometimes needs 'this ugly wart that sits on the side'. The strategy layer's job is to 'get out of [the combat's] way'. Also: they should have cut bad design faster and noticed what the game's constraints were imposing.

title: Matthew Davis, Into the Breach Design Postmortem (GDC 2019) [59:00]
label: developer
claim: How they found problems: for teaching and raw usability they did a lot of playtesting; for earlier decisions they mostly tested on themselves ('a lot of intuition'), and he admits he lacks a better answer.
